sources: Dairy Farmers Handbook, 9th ed. 2025, Farmers Helping Farmers/UPEI
Smallholder Dairy Farmer Training Manual, ILRI Manual 24, 2016

rules.name: Mild heat stress — THI 72–77
rules.risk: THI 72–77 causes mild heat stress in dairy cows. Milk production drops 5–10%. Cows show increased respiration and reduced feed intake.
actions: Provide at least 4 sq m of shade per cow — check existing shade structures
Increase water supply by 30 L/cow/day above normal (total ~120 L/cow/day)
Move feeding to cooler hours — early morning (5–7 am) and evening (after 6 pm)
Ensure good ventilation in housing — open side panels, check airflow
Plant or extend shade trees on the windward side of the paddock
preventive_actions: Install shade structures before June — at least 4 sq m per cow
Plant fast-growing shade trees (Grevillea, Leucaena) on the south and west sides
Fit water troughs with automatic refill floats to handle peak demand

rules.name: Severe heat stress — THI ≥ 78
rules.risk: THI ≥ 78 is severe heat stress. Milk production drops 15–25%. Conception rates fall 20–30%. Risk of hyperthermia and heat exhaustion in high-yielding cows.
actions: Emergency cooling: move cows to shade immediately — do not leave in open paddock
Wet cows with cool water and use fans if available — focus on flank and udder
Provide cool, clean water continuously — 100+ L/cow available at all times
Feed only during coolest hours (4–7 am and after 7 pm) — remove stale feed
Delay any AI or breeding procedures — conception rate severely compromised
Expect milk yield loss of 15–25% — adjust farm income projections
Watch for any cow standing apart, panting excessively, or off feed — call vet if rectal temp > 40°C
preventive_actions: Install shade and ventilation before hot season
Fit automatic water refill systems to all troughs
Synchronise AI to coolest months of year

rules.name: Severe heat stress in peak dry season — THI ≥ 78, June–August
rules.risk: THI ≥ 78 during June–August (long dry season) is the highest-risk heat stress period. Forage is also scarce, compounding nutritional and heat stress simultaneously.
actions: Emergency cooling measures — shade, water wetting, fans if available
Draw on silage or hay reserves now — forage scarcity will worsen heat stress impact
Provide 100+ L/cow/day cool water — prioritise high-yielding cows
Delay all AI and breeding until September when temperatures moderate
Increase dairy meal ration to compensate for reduced forage intake: (milk kg − 5) ÷ 2 = kg meal/day
Monitor for signs of heat exhaustion: rectal temp > 40°C, excessive panting — call vet immediately
preventive_actions: Build silage stocks before June to buffer both forage shortage and heat period
Ensure shade structures are in place before long dry season

rules.name: High daytime temperature — max > 32°C
rules.risk: Maximum temperatures above 32°C elevate heat load on dairy cows, particularly during afternoon milking. Freshly calved cows and high-yielders are most vulnerable.
actions: Move afternoon milking to earlier — before 1 pm if possible to avoid peak heat
Provide at least 4 sq m shade per cow — check structures for integrity
Increase water availability — ensure trough capacity of 100 L per cow per day
Reduce herd density in housing during afternoon hours — open all ventilation panels
Check on freshly calved cows and high-yielders specifically during peak afternoon heat
preventive_actions: Install shade and ventilation before dry season
Plant shade trees on the west and south sides of paddocks

rules.name: High temperature combined with humidity — max > 32°C and RH > 70%
rules.risk: High temperature combined with humidity above 70% prevents evaporative cooling in cows. This is more dangerous than dry heat alone. Hyperthermia risk is high.
actions: Emergency cooling: wet cows with cool water — evaporation is limited but water cooling still works
Ensure maximum airflow — fans essential in this condition, open all housing sides
Provide 100+ L/cow/day cool water — change water in troughs twice daily if possible
Delay AI, embryo transfers, and any stressful procedures
Watch all cows closely — this condition can rapidly progress to fatal hyperthermia
If rectal temperature > 40.5°C: call veterinarian immediately and apply continuous cooling
preventive_actions: Install mechanical ventilation (fans) before onset of hot humid season
Avoid high-humidity housing designs — raised slatted floors aid evaporation

rules.name: Heat stress compounded by dry spell — THI ≥ 72 and dry > 7 days
rules.risk: Heat stress combined with an extended dry spell means both cooling (evaporation from soil and plants) and water supply are compromised. Forage quality also declines.
actions: Check and top up all water sources — troughs, tanks, streams — water demand surges in heat
Begin drawing on hay or silage reserves — pasture quality and quantity is declining
Provide shade and ensure adequate ventilation in housing
Increase dairy meal to compensate for reduced pasture quantity: (milk kg − 5) ÷ 2 = kg meal/day
Monitor body condition score — do not let cows lose more than half a condition score/month
preventive_actions: Maintain emergency forage reserves of at least 30 days feed before dry season
Have alternative water sources identified before dry season

rules.name: Severe heat stress at start of long dry season — THI ≥ 78, May–July
rules.risk: THI ≥ 78 in May–July coincides with the start of Kenya's long dry season. Pasture declines rapidly, worsening nutritional stress alongside heat stress.
actions: Activate silage and hay reserves immediately — do not wait until pasture is exhausted
Emergency cooling: shade, wetting, fans if available
Provide 100+ L/cow/day cool water
Delay AI and breeding — conception rates severely reduced at THI ≥ 78
Increase dairy meal to compensate: (milk kg − 5) ÷ 2 = kg meal/day
Monitor all cows daily for signs of heat exhaustion — prioritise high-yielders and freshly calved cows
preventive_actions: Complete AI program before May — target calving in cooler months
Build forage reserves (silage, hay) before start of May

rules.name: Warm nights — minimum temperature > 22°C
rules.risk: Cows need overnight cooling to recover from daytime heat load. When night temperatures stay above 22°C, cows cannot recover between milkings, leading to cumulative stress.
actions: Ensure maximum ventilation overnight — leave all housing panels open
Check that water troughs are full before sunset — cows drink heavily at night in warm conditions
Consider early morning milking (4–5 am) when cows are coolest
Monitor cumulative milk loss over several warm nights — 3+ consecutive warm nights = take action
preventive_actions: Design housing for cross-ventilation — East-West orientation for prevailing breeze
Avoid overstocking housing — 6 sq m/cow minimum floor space

rules.name: Mastitis risk — rain and high humidity
rules.risk: Wet, humid conditions cause muddy housing, dirty udders, and moisture accumulation in teat orifices — the classic mastitis entry route. Streptococcus, Staphylococcus, and E. coli infections all peak in wet conditions.
actions: Check all housing drainage — standing water must not pool in stalls
Add dry bedding (sawdust, dry grass) — minimum 10 cm depth under cows
Apply teat pre-dip AND post-dip at every milking — do not skip either
Check udder and teats daily for swelling, heat, or clots in milk
Dry off any cow showing mastitis signs after consulting vet — do not milk through infection
preventive_actions: Ensure drainage channels are cleared before each rainy season
Apply dry cow therapy (DCT) at dry-off — reduces subclinical mastitis risk in next lactation
Maintain teat scoring records to identify high-risk animals
sources: Smallholder Dairy Farmer Training Manual, ILRI Manual 24, 2016

rules.name: Mastitis risk — extended wet period (> 3 consecutive wet days)
rules.risk: More than 3 consecutive wet days means continuously wet housing, persistent mud at the paddock entrance, and cows unable to find dry resting areas. Mastitis incidence increases significantly after 3+ wet days.
actions: Bring cows into housing during heavy rain — prevent standing in wet paddock
Replace all wet bedding with dry material — this is non-negotiable
Apply teat pre-dip and post-dip at every milking — iodine-based post-dip is most effective
Inspect teats for wet chapping — apply barrier teat dip if skin is cracked
Conduct a CMT (California Mastitis Test) on all cows this week
preventive_actions: Install concrete feeding pad at housing entrance to prevent mud buildup
Apply DCT at dry-off — wet conditions make this especially important

rules.name: Mastitis risk — sudden temperature change with rain
rules.risk: A sudden temperature drop combined with rain creates acute stress on the cow's immune system, temporarily reducing resistance to mastitis pathogens.
actions: Shelter cows from rain and cold wind — close windward side of housing
Maintain rigorous pre-dip and post-dip routine at milking
Watch for any cows off feed or showing udder swelling in the next 48 hours
Check bedding — ensure cows have dry, warm resting area
preventive_actions: Ensure all cows are up to date on teat condition scoring
Review milking hygiene protocol with all milkers

rules.name: Dry-off mastitis risk — rain during October–November
rules.risk: October–November short rains coincide with the drying-off period for cows that calved in Jan–Feb. Wet conditions at dry-off dramatically increase subclinical mastitis risk in the subsequent lactation.
actions: Apply dry cow therapy (DCT) antibiotic tubes at dry-off — mandatory in wet conditions
Apply teat sealant after DCT tube to physically block teat orifice
Inspect udder daily for first 2 weeks after dry-off — look for swelling, heat, or discharge
Keep dry cows in dry, well-bedded housing — not wet paddock
Maintain pre-dip and post-dip at last milking before dry-off
preventive_actions: Schedule dry-off timing to avoid peak rainy season where possible
Maintain mastitis records to identify which cows need intramammary treatment at dry-off

rules.name: Mastitis risk — cool moist conditions (15–25°C, RH > 85%)
rules.risk: Cool moist conditions (15–25°C at RH > 85%) are optimal for Streptococcus agalactiae and Streptococcus uberis — the most common environmental mastitis pathogens in Kenya.
actions: Maintain strict pre-dip and post-dip at every milking — do not skip in this weather
Increase bedding replacement frequency — wet bedding harbours pathogens
Check teat condition — soft, overhydrated teat skin from humidity increases infection risk
Conduct a CMT (California Mastitis Test) on all cows this week
Ensure milking equipment is functioning correctly — teat-end impact is a major mastitis driver
preventive_actions: Keep drainage channels clear during long rains
Apply lime to housing floor monthly during wet season to reduce pathogen load
sources: Smallholder Dairy Farmer Training Manual, ILRI Manual 24, 2016

rules.name: Mastitis risk — heavy rainfall (> 10 mm today)
rules.risk: Heavy rainfall (>10 mm) causes rapid onset of wet, dirty housing and paddock conditions. Teats are splashed with contaminated water and mud, dramatically increasing mastitis pathogen contact.
actions: Keep cows under cover during and immediately after heavy rain
Clean teats with individual disposable wipes before milking — do not use shared cloth
Apply teat pre-dip and post-dip at every milking today
Clear drainage channels around housing — check for pooling before bedtime
Add dry bedding after rain stops — wet concrete is a mastitis risk
preventive_actions: Install rain guttering on housing roof to direct water away from the housing area
Raise floor level in housing above surrounding paddock to prevent rainwater ingress

rules.name: Respiratory disease alert — rapid temperature drop
rules.risk: A temperature drop > 8°C within 24 hours is a major trigger for Bovine Respiratory Disease (BRD) — especially in calves. Draughts combined with cold stress cause rapid onset pneumonia.
actions: Check all calves immediately — respiratory disease kills calves within 24–48 hours if untreated
Close all draughts in calf housing — use sacks, boards, or tarpaulin
Add extra dry bedding in calf pens — calves must be able to nest in bedding
Monitor adult cows for coughing or nasal discharge — call vet if multiple cows affected
Separate any sick calves immediately — BRD spreads rapidly in cold, wet conditions
Check temperature of calves under 3 months — rectal temp < 38°C indicates hypothermia
preventive_actions: Vaccinate calves for IBR and PI-3 before cold season
Ensure calf housing has no through-draughts at calf height — site openings high on walls
sources: Smallholder Dairy Farmer Training Manual, ILRI Manual 24, 2016

rules.name: Calf cold and respiratory risk — cold night with wind (min < 12°C, wind > 15 km/h)
rules.risk: Cold wind at night (below 12°C with wind above 15 km/h) creates dangerous wind chill for calves. Calves under 2 weeks old are at high risk of hypothermia and pneumonia.
actions: Check calf pens for wind penetration — block draughts at calf level with boards or sacking
Add extra dry bedding — calves should be able to sit with bedding above their knees
Consider calf jackets for calves under 2 weeks old
Check colostrum feeding records — calves that received inadequate colostrum are most at risk
Adult cows also at risk — ensure housing is closed on windward side tonight
preventive_actions: Ensure calf housing windbreaks are in place before cold season
Check that newborn calves receive at least 2 L colostrum within 30 minutes of birth

rules.name: Calf pneumonia risk — cold night with rain (min < 12°C, rain > 2 mm)
rules.risk: Cold rainy nights are the highest-risk conditions for calf pneumonia. Wet calves cannot thermoregulate and rapidly develop respiratory infections.
actions: Ensure all calves are housed and dry overnight — bring any outdoor calves in immediately
Dry any wet calves with a towel — wet calves lose heat 5x faster than dry calves
Check for signs of pneumonia: cough, nasal discharge, fast breathing (> 30 breaths/min), off feed
Call vet if any calf shows respiratory symptoms — prompt antibiotic treatment is critical
Close all rain-facing openings in calf housing
preventive_actions: Design calf housing so that rain cannot blow in — covered, raised pen with windbreaks
Vaccinate calves for respiratory pathogens (IBR, BVD, PI-3, BRSV) before cold season
sources: Smallholder Dairy Farmer Training Manual, ILRI Manual 24, 2016

rules.name: Cold stress risk — minimum temperature below 10°C
rules.risk: Temperatures below 10°C require calves to divert energy from growth to thermoregulation. Milk intake increases but growth rates drop. Pneumonia risk is elevated for all calves under 3 months.
actions: Check all calves for early respiratory signs: cough, snotty nose, dullness, off feed
Ensure adequate dry bedding depth in calf pens — minimum 15 cm deep, changed every 3–4 days
Increase milk or milk replacer feeding by 10% in cold conditions
Vaccinate any unvaccinated calves for IBR and PI-3 if not already done
Make sure all housing openings at calf height are blocked on the windward side
preventive_actions: Vaccinate all calves before cold season
Ensure colostrum records are complete — inadequate colostrum is the greatest risk factor

rules.name: Dusty conditions respiratory risk — extended dry spell with wind (dry > 14 days, wind > 20 km/h)
rules.risk: Extended dry conditions with strong wind create high ambient dust levels. Dust particles irritate the bovine respiratory tract, increasing susceptibility to viral and bacterial pneumonia.
actions: Wet down the housing area and paddock entrances to reduce dust
Check that cattle are not being fed dry hay in dusty conditions — soak hay first
Ensure housing has adequate airflow to dilute dust without creating draughts
Watch for increased coughing or nasal discharge across the herd
preventive_actions: Plant grass cover crops around housing to prevent dust accumulation
Maintain windbreaks to reduce wind speed within the farmyard

rules.name: Respiratory risk — rain with wind (rain > 3 mm, wind > 20 km/h)
rules.risk: Driving rain at high wind speed drenches animals and creates rapid heat loss. This combination is a classic BRD trigger, especially for younger and freshly calved animals.
actions: Bring calves under 3 months old inside immediately
Close the windward side of all housing to block driving rain
Check freshly calved cows and high-yielders — these animals are most susceptible
Dry any wet calves with towels or sacking
Monitor all animals for coughing and nasal discharge over the next 24–48 hours
preventive_actions: Install windbreaks on prevailing wind side of all housing
Ensure housing has movable panels for flexible management of driving rain events

rules.name: Tick-borne disease risk — rain and warm temperatures (72h rain > 20 mm, temp 15–30°C)
rules.risk: Rain followed by warm temperatures triggers tick egg hatching and larval emergence. East Coast Fever (ECF/Theileria), Anaplasmosis, and Babesiosis all peak 2–4 weeks after wet, warm conditions.
actions: Spray all cattle with acaricide within 48 hours — do not delay
Check all cattle daily for tick attachment sites: ears, neck, groin, tail base, udder
Record tick burden score (0–5) per animal to track population trend
Watch for ECF signs 2–4 weeks after this event: swollen lymph nodes, high fever (>40°C), off feed
Remove any engorged ticks by hand from sensitive areas (teats, ears) in addition to spraying
preventive_actions: Rotate acaricide class every 3 months to prevent tick resistance
Vaccinate calves for ECF (ITM or infection-and-treatment method) before first rain season
Remove tall grass in and around paddocks to reduce tick habitat
sources: Smallholder Dairy Farmer Training Manual, ILRI Manual 24, 2016

rules.name: Tick and fly vector alert — extended wet period and warmth (wet days > 5, temp > 15°C)
rules.risk: More than 5 consecutive wet days at temperatures above 15°C creates ideal conditions for tick larvae, tsetse fly, and stable fly populations. Trypanosomiasis risk also elevated in tsetse-affected areas.
actions: Increase acaricide spraying frequency to every 5–7 days during extended wet, warm period
Inspect all animals daily for tick attachment — especially around ears, udder, and groin
Check for signs of tick-borne disease: lethargy, high fever, reduced milk, swollen lymph nodes
Remove stagnant water — empty tyres, buckets, any containers that collect water — fly breeding sites
Apply pyrethroid pour-on along the back if fly burden is visible
preventive_actions: Drain low-lying wet areas in and around paddocks
Maintain pasture rotation to break tick life cycle

rules.name: Peak tick emergence after heavy rain — 72h rain > 30 mm, temp 20–30°C
rules.risk: Very heavy rain (>30 mm in 72h) at optimal tick development temperatures (20–30°C) causes mass tick hatching and questing. This is the highest-risk single event for ECF and anaplasmosis outbreaks.
actions: Spray all cattle with acaricide today — this is the most critical prophylactic window
Inspect all animals for tick attachment — check all body regions including inside ears
Alert neighbouring farmers — coordinated acaricide treatment in a community reduces reinfestation
Watch for ECF signs 2–3 weeks from now: swollen parotid lymph node, lacrimation, high fever
If ECF vaccination has not been done this season: contact vet for emergency ITM vaccination
preventive_actions: Ensure ECF vaccination is current for all animals before rainy season
Stock acaricide in advance before onset of long rains
sources: Smallholder Dairy Farmer Training Manual, ILRI Manual 24, 2016

rules.name: Long rains tick season — March–May, temperature 18–28°C
rules.risk: March–May long rains at warm temperatures are the primary tick season in Kenya. ECF, anaplasmosis, and babesiosis outbreaks peak during and after this period.
actions: Increase acaricide spraying to at least every 7 days during March–May
Check all animals daily for tick attachment — pay special attention to ears and udder
Ensure ECF vaccination is current for all cattle
Record milk yield daily — unexplained drop in yield is an early sign of tick-borne disease
Have treatment drugs stocked: oxytetracycline for anaplasmosis, buparvaquone (Butalex) for ECF
preventive_actions: Vaccinate calves for ECF before March
Rotate pastures to prevent tick population buildup in any single paddock

rules.name: Short rains tick season — October–November, temperature 18–28°C
rules.risk: October–November short rains with warm temperatures constitute the second annual tick season. Animals that survived the long rains may have reduced immunity — reinfestation is dangerous.
actions: Resume weekly acaricide spraying from October 1
Check animals for tick attachment daily — especially animals that were not treated regularly in dry season
Review acaricide records — rotate to a different class if same product used all year
Stock treatment drugs before season: oxytetracycline, Butalex (buparvaquone)
Inspect animals for condition score — animals in poor condition are more susceptible to tick-borne disease
preventive_actions: Book ECF booster vaccinations before October if recommended by vet
Clear paddock vegetation before short rains to reduce tick questing habitat

rules.name: Post-drought first rain — tick questing surge (dry > 336 hours, rain today > 5 mm)
rules.risk: After more than 14 days without rain, the first significant rainfall triggers synchronised tick questing (host-seeking). Tick populations that survived drought emerge simultaneously — very high exposure risk.
actions: Apply acaricide spray within 24 hours of first significant rain after dry spell
Inspect all animals today for any already-attached ticks from drought survivors
Alert herd owner: tick-borne disease risk elevated for next 3–4 weeks after first rain
Do not move cattle to new paddocks immediately after first rain — tick reinfestation risk
preventive_actions: Apply prophylactic acaricide during last week of dry spell, before rains arrive
Identify and clear tall grass areas before rain season

rules.name: Fly and tick vector season — warm, humid, rainy months (temp 15–30°C, RH > 70%)
rules.risk: Warm temperatures with high humidity during the rainy months create optimal conditions for both ticks and biting flies (stable fly, horn fly). Combined vector pressure increases disease transmission risk.
actions: Inspect all animals for tick load at least every 3 days during this period
Apply acaricide on a regular schedule — at minimum every 10 days
Remove stagnant water around housing — essential for fly population control
Apply pyrethroid pour-on for fly control if fly annoyance is causing production loss
Record any unexplained fever or drop in milk yield — early signs of vector-borne disease
preventive_actions: Ensure drainage is working before onset of rainy season
Rotate grazing paddocks to prevent tick population concentration

rules.name: Heavy cumulative rainfall — broad tick and vector alert (7-day rain > 50 mm)
rules.risk: More than 50 mm in 7 days saturates the soil and creates widespread ideal tick and fly breeding habitat across the farm. Pastures will remain tick-infested for weeks after rain stops.
actions: Maintain weekly acaricide spraying — do not reduce frequency even if individual tick burden looks low
Pastures used this week will remain tick-infested for 3–4 weeks minimum
Inspect all animals twice weekly for tick attachment
Check for signs of tick-borne disease across the herd: fever, milk drop, swollen lymph nodes
preventive_actions: Paddock rotation: avoid returning cattle to same paddock within 3 weeks during wet season
Slash and clear vegetation after heavy rains — reduces tick questing sites

rules.name: Internal parasite (worm) risk — extended dry spell (dry > 30 days)
rules.risk: Extended dry periods concentrate worm larvae in remaining green patches and water points. Animals graze intensively around these sites, leading to high worm ingestion. Post-drought parasite burdens can be severe.
actions: Conduct strategic deworming at end of dry spell — before rains arrive and larvae explode
Weigh all animals and dose by bodyweight — never by estimate
Perform a faecal egg count (FEC) if possible — use results to prioritise which animals to treat
Move animals away from heavily grazed water-point areas where larvae concentrate
Check body condition score — animals losing condition in dry season may have high worm burden
preventive_actions: Rotate pastures to prevent worm larval buildup on any single paddock
Deworm strategically — not on fixed calendar but based on FEC and body condition
sources: Smallholder Dairy Farmer Training Manual, ILRI Manual 24, 2016

rules.name: Worm development conditions — rain and warmth (72h rain > 15 mm, temp > 18°C)
rules.risk: Rain (>15 mm in 72h) at temperatures above 18°C accelerates development of worm eggs to infective larvae on pasture. Larvae are available for ingestion 2–3 weeks after rain.
actions: Assess need for deworming in 3–4 weeks by monitoring faecal egg count or body condition
Rotate pastures now to allow currently used paddocks to rest — larvae on resting paddocks die over 4–6 weeks
Check calves and young stock closely — they are most susceptible to worm challenge after rain
Look for signs of worm burden in 2–3 weeks: diarrhoea, bottle jaw, weight loss, poor coat
preventive_actions: Avoid grazing same paddock for more than 3 consecutive weeks during wet season
Maintain browse species (Leucaena, Calliandra) in pasture — condensed tannins reduce worm burden

rules.name: Strategic deworming month — May or November
rules.risk: May (end of long rains) and November (end of short rains) are the two peak periods for internal parasite infection in Kenyan dairy cattle. Treating now prevents post-rain worm burden buildup.
actions: Conduct strategic deworming this month — end of rainy season is the optimal treatment window
Use faecal egg count (FEC) to select which animals to treat — do not blanket-treat unless warranted
Weigh all cattle and dose accurately by bodyweight — under-dosing promotes anthelmintic resistance
Rotate to a different anthelmintic class if the same drug was used last time
Include liver fluke (Fasciola hepatica) treatment if the farm has wet, low-lying areas
preventive_actions: Keep deworming records — date, product, dose, animals treated, and FEC results
Control liver fluke (Fasciola) by draining wet areas and treating with triclabendazole
sources: Smallholder Dairy Farmer Training Manual, ILRI Manual 24, 2016

rules.name: Liver fluke (Fasciola) risk — extended wet period (wet > 7 days, temp 18–28°C)
rules.risk: More than 7 consecutive wet days at 18–28°C creates ideal conditions for Lymnaea snails — the intermediate host of Fasciola hepatica (liver fluke). Fluke infection follows 6–8 weeks after snail activity.
actions: Restrict access to wet, low-lying paddocks and around water bodies where snails breed
Check for signs of liver fluke 6–8 weeks from now: bottle jaw, poor condition, reduced milk yield
Include liver fluke treatment (triclabendazole) in the next deworming round
Drain any permanently wet areas in paddocks if possible — removes snail habitat permanently
preventive_actions: Map wet areas on the farm — fence off permanently wet zones to prevent cattle access
Treat with triclabendazole twice yearly (after long rains and after short rains)

rules.name: Forage scarcity — dry spell > 21 days
rules.risk: After 21 dry days, pasture quality and quantity decline significantly. Crude protein content falls as grasses mature and dry out. Milk yield will drop unless supplementation is increased.
actions: Increase dairy meal supplementation: calculate (milk kg − 5) ÷ 2 = kg meal per day
Begin drawing on silage or hay reserves — do not wait until pasture is exhausted
Assess remaining forage supply: count days of reserve at current consumption rate
Reduce grazing time in heavily depleted paddocks — allow recovery before rains
Provide mineral lick or loose mineral supplement — dry season increases mineral deficiency risk
preventive_actions: Build minimum 30 days of emergency forage reserve before each dry season
Grow drought-tolerant forages: Brachiaria, Rhodes grass, or Sorghum-Sudan hybrids
sources: Smallholder Dairy Farmer Training Manual, ILRI Manual 24, 2016

rules.name: Severe forage shortage — dry spell > 42 days
rules.risk: Six weeks without rain means severe forage shortage. Pasture is dried out and nutritionally depleted. Cows are at risk of significant body condition loss, reduced fertility, and depressed milk production.
actions: Immediately calculate feed budget: litres milk per day × 0.45 kg meal = absolute minimum meal needed
Begin rationing silage/hay — if reserves are critically low, source emergency forage now
Reduce stocking rate if necessary — sell non-productive animals to reduce feed demand
Provide protein supplement (sunflower cake, cotton seed cake) — dry pasture is protein-deficient
Check body condition score on all cows — do not allow score to fall below 2.5
Ensure water availability — dehydration worsens nutritional stress
preventive_actions: Build 60+ days of emergency forage reserve before long dry season
Plant perennial deep-rooted forages (Brachiaria brizantha cv. Mulato) that withstand drought

rules.name: Nutritional support during heat stress — THI > 72
rules.risk: Heat-stressed cows reduce dry matter intake by 10–25% while energy requirements increase due to panting. This nutritional gap directly reduces milk yield and fertility.
actions: Increase energy density of ration — add bypass fat or concentrate if available
Feed during cooler hours (early morning and evening) — do not feed during afternoon heat peak
Ensure access to clean, cool water at all times — feed intake drops if water is warm
Adjust dairy meal: (milk kg − 5) ÷ 2 = kg meal/day — may need to increase above this baseline
Provide electrolyte supplement if cows are panting heavily (sweating losses in heat)
preventive_actions: Plan ration increases for hot months in the annual feed budget
Stock bypass fat before onset of hot season

rules.name: Early dry season nutrition alert — dry > 14 days
rules.risk: After 14 dry days, pasture quality is declining. Grasses transition from vegetative (high protein, high energy) to mature/dry (low protein, high fibre). Supplementation should begin now, before yield drop becomes visible.
actions: Begin supplementary feeding — add 1–2 kg dairy meal per cow per day above maintenance
Assess silage and hay stocks — project consumption for remaining dry season
Implement rotational grazing — rest each paddock for at least 3 weeks
Check water quality — dry season can concentrate minerals in bore water
preventive_actions: Identify dry-season feed sources (hay, silage, crop residues, stover) before dry season
Establish crop residue agreements with neighbouring crop farmers before harvest

rules.name: First rain after dry spell — grazing management (rain > 10 mm after dry > 14 days)
rules.risk: After a dry spell, the first heavy rain triggers rapid new grass growth. However, very young grass (< 10 cm) is high in water and low in dry matter — grazing too early reduces intake and can cause bloat.
actions: Hold cattle off freshly rained paddocks for at least 7 days to allow grass to reach 15+ cm
Continue supplementary feeding until new pasture is at adequate height
Watch for bloat when cattle are first turned onto lush, rapidly growing pasture
Graze rested paddocks first — they have the highest quality regrowth
Consider topping overgrown paddocks before regrazing if dry season growth became rank
preventive_actions: Plan grazing rotation before rains arrive — map paddock rest periods in advance
Keep anti-bloat drench (poloxalene) on hand for first grazing of lush pastures
sources: Smallholder Dairy Farmer Training Manual, ILRI Manual 24, 2016

rules.name: Cold weather nutrition — increased energy needs (min < 12°C)
rules.risk: Temperatures below 12°C increase maintenance energy requirements in cattle. Cows divert energy from milk production to thermoregulation unless ration is increased.
actions: Increase dairy meal ration by 0.5–1 kg/cow/day during cold nights (below 12°C)
Ensure ad-libitum access to high-quality roughage — hay or silage at night in cold conditions
Check water trough temperature — cattle drink less from very cold water troughs, reducing intake
Watch for weight loss in calves — they have the highest cold-related energy demand
preventive_actions: Plan extra meal reserves for cold highland periods (June–August in central Kenya highlands)
Ensure housing provides adequate windbreak to reduce cold stress

rules.name: Increased water demand — heat stress (THI ≥ 72)
rules.risk: At THI ≥ 72, dairy cows increase water intake by up to 30 L/day above normal. Inadequate water supply during heat stress rapidly leads to dehydration, reduced milk, and increased rectal temperature.
actions: Increase water supply by at least 30 L/cow/day above baseline (total 90–120 L/cow/day)
Check that all troughs are full and automatic refill is working
Provide water near feed — cows drink mainly within 30 minutes of eating
Ensure water temperature is below 20°C — warm water reduces voluntary intake
Check for competition at water troughs — dominant cows can restrict access for others
preventive_actions: Install trough capacity of at least 100 L per 10 cows
Fit automatic ball-valve refill on all troughs before hot season

rules.name: Critical water demand — severe heat stress (THI ≥ 78)
rules.risk: At THI ≥ 78, cows require 100+ L/cow/day of water. Inadequate supply within hours leads to severe dehydration, hyperthermia, and potentially fatal heat exhaustion in high-yielding cows.
actions: Ensure 100+ L of cool water per cow per day is available at all times
Change water in troughs twice daily to maintain cool temperature (target < 20°C)
Provide multiple water access points — dominant cows block subordinates at single troughs
Use water to wet/cool cows directly if available — wetting reduces rectal temperature faster than drinking
Monitor all cows for dehydration signs: dry muzzle, skin tenting, sunken eyes — call vet if present
preventive_actions: Install supplementary water storage (tanks) with capacity for 3+ days' peak demand
Identify and secure backup water sources before hot season

rules.name: High water demand — hot day (max > 32°C)
rules.risk: Maximum temperatures above 32°C significantly increase evaporative water loss in cattle. Water intake can reach 80–100 L/cow/day on hot days.
actions: Check all water troughs this morning — ensure they are full before peak heat (11 am–3 pm)
Provide shade near water troughs — cows will stand near water source in hot conditions
Move milking to cooler hours if water supply is limited — reduces peak water demand at milking time
Top up trough supply in the afternoon if automatic refill is not available
preventive_actions: Fit automatic ball-valve refill systems on all troughs
Install troughs in shaded locations — direct sun heats water and reduces intake

rules.name: Water supply risk — extended dry spell (dry > 21 days)
rules.risk: After 21 dry days, streams, ponds, and shallow wells often decline in yield. Reduced water supply combined with dry season heat stress creates compounding risk of dehydration in the herd.
actions: Assess current water source levels — check stream flow, bore pump yield, or tank storage
Identify backup water sources in case primary source fails
Reduce non-essential water uses (washing down) to prioritise drinking water for cattle
Check water quality in remaining surface sources — concentration of algae and bacteria increases as water levels fall
If primary water source is at risk: contact water vendor or plan emergency supply now, not in a crisis
preventive_actions: Install rainwater harvesting before dry season — 10,000 L tank can bridge a 14-day shortage for 10 cows
Repair and deepen boreholes before onset of dry season
sources: Smallholder Dairy Farmer Training Manual, ILRI Manual 24, 2016

rules.name: AI conception risk — severe heat stress in breeding season (THI ≥ 78, June–August)
rules.risk: THI ≥ 78 during June–August reduces conception rate at AI by 20–30%. Oocyte quality is compromised 3–4 weeks before visible heat stress. AI performed in these conditions will have poor results.
actions: Delay AI until September when temperatures moderate — conception rates recover quickly after heat breaks
If AI cannot be delayed: perform at earliest morning opportunity (4–5 am) when THI is at daily minimum
Provide shade and cool water 48 hours before and after AI to minimise heat stress at insemination
Detect heat 3 times daily (morning, noon, evening) — heat expression is reduced in stressed cows
Consider progesterone CIDR synchronisation to overcome suppressed heat expression
preventive_actions: Plan AI calendar to target insemination in cooler months — calving in March–April optimises production
Synchronise herds to enable AI in October–November short dry season

rules.name: Newborn calf hypothermia risk — cold nights in calving season (min < 10°C, Feb–March)
rules.risk: February–March calving season with nights below 10°C creates high hypothermia risk for newborn calves. A newborn calf that cannot thermoregulate within 2 hours of birth is at high risk of death.
actions: Check all heavily pregnant cows at night — calves born in cold conditions need immediate attention
Dry newborn calves with a towel immediately after birth — wet calves chill within minutes
Bring newborn calves indoors or into a sheltered, bedded pen immediately after birth
Feed 2 L of colostrum within 30 minutes of birth — colostrum provides calories for thermoregulation
Check rectal temperature of newborn: below 37°C requires emergency warming (warm water bath or heat lamp)
Monitor dam closely for retained placenta or metritis in cold conditions
preventive_actions: Prepare warm, dry calving pen before February — dry bedding and windproof
Have towels, heat lamp, and colostrum on standby during calving season
sources: Smallholder Dairy Farmer Training Manual, ILRI Manual 24, 2016

rules.name: Calving emergency — cold wet conditions at calving (rain > 5 mm, min < 14°C, Feb–March)
rules.risk: Cold wet conditions during calving season are the most dangerous combination for newborn calf survival. A wet calf in rain at 12°C can become hypothermic within 15 minutes of birth.
actions: Move all heavily pregnant cows into the calving pen NOW — do not leave in wet paddock
Check for calving cows every 2 hours day and night during this weather
Dry the calf immediately with a towel — then move into warm, dry pen
Feed 2 L colostrum within 30 minutes of birth — do not wait for the calf to stand
If calf cannot suckle: tube-feed colostrum using an oesophageal feeder
Watch dam for signs of milk fever, retained placenta, or prolapse — cold wet conditions increase risk
preventive_actions: Ensure calving pen is dry, sheltered, and bedded before February
Have emergency colostrum (frozen or replacement) available before calving season

rules.name: Heat stress reduces AI success — THI ≥ 72 in breeding season (June–August)
rules.risk: THI 72–77 during June–August reduces conception rate at AI by 10–15%. Heat stress also suppresses behavioural oestrus, making heat detection harder.
actions: Detect heat at minimum 3 times daily — morning (5 am), midday, and evening (6 pm)
Perform AI in early morning when cow temperature is lowest — ideally before 8 am
Ensure shade and cool water are available 48 hours before and after AI
Record conception results carefully — if < 50% conception rate, consider waiting for cooler months
Use tail paint or activity monitors to improve heat detection accuracy
preventive_actions: Plan AI program calendar to avoid peak heat months where possible
Consider synchronisation protocol timed to a predicted cooler period

rules.name: Acaricide spraying blocked — rain expected (rain probability next 6h > 40%)
rules.risk: Rain within 6 hours of acaricide application washes product off the animal before it is absorbed, providing no tick control while wasting product and money.
actions: Do not apply acaricide today if rain probability > 40% in next 6 hours
Reschedule spraying to the next dry morning — ideally before 9 am when conditions are calm
If tick burden is critical and spraying cannot wait: apply acaricide in an evening window after rain risk passes
Check 24-hour forecast for the best dry window in the next 2 days
preventive_actions: Plan acaricide schedule around weather forecast — check rain probability before spraying
Maintain records of spray dates to ensure animals are not unprotected for more than 14 days
sources: Smallholder Dairy Farmer Training Manual, ILRI Manual 24, 2016

rules.name: Acaricide spraying blocked — high wind (wind > 15 km/h)
rules.risk: Wind above 15 km/h causes spray drift, resulting in uneven coverage, missed tick attachment sites, and off-target contamination. Operators also inhale drifting product.
actions: Do not spray acaricide when wind exceeds 15 km/h — delay until wind calms
Best spray window is early morning (6–9 am) when wind is typically lightest
If animals must be treated urgently: use pour-on acaricide applied directly to backline — less drift-sensitive
Stand upwind of the animal when spraying — protect yourself from chemical exposure
preventive_actions: Check wind speed before every spray session
Keep pour-on acaricide as backup option for windy or wet conditions

rules.name: Acaricide spraying blocked — rainfall today (rain > 2 mm)
rules.risk: Rainfall on the day of spraying washes acaricide off before it is effective. The animal will be unprotected while ticks are most active (tick populations surge after rain).
actions: Do not spray acaricide today — product will be washed off by rain
Reschedule for the next dry morning with < 2 mm rain forecast
If tick burden is severe and cannot wait: use pour-on acaricide applied under cover — less rain-sensitive than spraying
Hand-remove any engorged ticks from sensitive areas (teats, ears) as an emergency measure today
preventive_actions: Always check rain forecast before scheduling acaricide spraying
Stock pour-on acaricide for use on days when dip or spray tank is impractical due to rain
